sections.title: A Request Is Data Before It Is Traffic
sections.body:
A request is **a value** long before it is traffic: a method, a URL, a set of headers and a body, all of them ordinary JavaScript data. Building that value in one small function puts the interesting decisions - which header carries the token, what the default method is, how a base URL and a path join without doubling the slash - somewhere you can call a thousand times without a server.

Authentication is one of those decisions. A bearer token travels in the `Authorization` header as the literal text `Bearer ` followed by the token, and a client with no token must leave the header out entirely rather than send `Bearer undefined` and collect a 401 it cannot explain.

- A header that does not apply is an **absent key**, never an empty one.
- Headers are a plain object, so adding one is an assignment.

annotations.text: Accept is unconditional - it is what the client always wants back, regardless of who is asking.
An empty-string token is the case that catches people: it is falsy, but it is still a string, and `Bearer ` with nothing after it is worse than no header at all.
Content-Type describes the body you are sending. No body, no header - a GET that announces a JSON body is lying.
Strip every trailing slash from the base, then guarantee exactly one at the front of the path.
Both sides bring a slash here and neither brings one on the next line; both must produce the same URL.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `authHeaders(token)` returning the request headers object. It always carries `Accept: "application/json"`, and it carries `Authorization: "Bearer " + token` **only** when `token` is a non-empty string.
checkpoint.explain: An absent header and an empty one are different requests on the wire. `Authorization: Bearer ` with nothing after it is a credential the server must reject, while no header at all is an anonymous request it can answer or refuse cleanly - so the guard has to rule out the empty string, not just `null`.

sections.title: Reading What Came Back
sections.body:
What comes back is a number and some text, and neither is trustworthy alone. **The status code decides the shape**: 2xx means the body is your data, 4xx means you asked wrongly, 5xx means the server broke at something that was not your fault.

`JSON.parse` throws on anything that is not JSON, and a failing proxy answers with an HTML error page, which is exactly that - so the parse belongs inside a `try`. A 204 carries no body at all, so parsing must be skipped rather than attempted on an empty string.

Normalising both outcomes into one of two shapes - `{ ok, status, data }` or `{ ok, status, error }` - means every caller writes a single `if` instead of a switch over status codes it will get wrong.

annotations.text: A 204 has no body. Guarding here is cheaper than discovering that JSON.parse("") throws.
The parse is the only line that can throw, so it is the only line inside the try.
A well-behaved API explains itself in the body; when it does not, the status code is the only message there is.
A gateway failure is where this pays off - HTML in, a described error out, and no SyntaxError escaping into the caller.

checkpoint.explain: `JSON.parse` is a parser, not a converter: it happily returns a bare number, and it throws on the empty string rather than handing back `null`. The last line is the one that shapes your API - `JSON.stringify` drops keys whose value is `undefined`, so a result that sets `error: undefined` on success does not carry an empty error field, it carries no such field at all.

sections.title: Retry Only What Might Succeed, and Not Forever
sections.body:
A retry is worth making only when the failure might not repeat. A 500 or a 503 is the server admitting it fell over, and a 429 is it asking you to slow down - both deserve another try. A 404 or a 401 will fail identically forever, so retrying them only multiplies the user's wait.

Two things stop a retry loop from becoming an attack on your own server: a **cap** on the number of attempts, and a **growing wait** between them. Doubling that wait - 100ms, then 200ms, then 400ms - is called **exponential backoff**, and capping it stops the curve from turning a retry into a nap.

annotations.text: 429 is the odd one out: a 4xx that is your fault and still worth retrying, because the server told you to wait rather than to stop.
Math.min is the cap. Without it the eighth retry waits 12.8 seconds and the user has already left.
Attempt numbers are 1-based, so the first wait is the base delay itself.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `attemptDelays(attempts)` returning the array of waits **between** that many tries, in milliseconds: 100 doubling each time, capped at 800. `attemptDelays(3)` is `[100, 200]` and `attemptDelays(1)` is `[]`.
checkpoint.explain: The waits sit between the tries, not after them, so n attempts need n-1 delays and a single attempt needs none - that off-by-one is the difference between a client that returns and one that sleeps on its way out. The cap is what turns an exponential curve into a schedule you could defend to a user watching a spinner.

sections.title: The Transport Is a Parameter
sections.body:
A client's one unavoidable side effect is the network call, so make it **a parameter**. `runRequest(transport, config)` never mentions `fetch`; it calls whatever function it was handed. Production hands it one built on `fetch`, and a test hands it one that returns `{ status: 503 }` on demand.

That is not a workaround for this sandbox, though the sandbox makes it unmissable - there is no network here at all. It is how a retry policy gets tested: no real server will produce two 503s and then a 200 for you, in a millisecond, identically every time. The real runner writes `await transport(request)`, and because `await` hands a plain value straight back, that one line drives a transport that answers at once and one that answers with a promise.

The same discipline applies to waiting. A runner that truly slept 700ms would make its own suite slow and its schedule invisible, so this one **returns the delays it would have waited** and lets the caller decide what to do with them.

annotations.text: The runner does not know what a transport is. It knows only that calling it gives back a response.
A fake transport is two lines. A real server that answers 200 on cue is a machine, a deploy and a bad afternoon.
And this is the one you could never arrange on purpose - a server that is reliably, repeatably down.
Same runner, same request, opposite outcome. Nothing inside the runner changed between the two calls.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `async function tryTwice(transport)`. Call `transport()` and `await` the result. If its `status` is 500 or above, call the transport once more and return that second `status`; otherwise return the first. The transport may answer with a plain object or with a promise.

tests.input: (function () { let i = 0; const seq = [{ status: 500 }, { status: 200 }]; return () => seq[i++]; })()
(function () { let i = 0; const seq = [{ status: 503 }, { status: 503 }]; return async () => seq[i++]; })()

checkpoint.explain: `await` on a plain value hands it straight back on the next tick, so one runner drives both an instant transport and a promise-returning one without a single type check. That is precisely what lets a test swap the network for a two-line arrow function while the code under test notices nothing at all.

trial.prompt:
**The Trial.** Build the pure core of a REST API client as five functions. There is no network in this sandbox and none in the tests - the transport is handed to your runner as an argument. The acceptance tests below are the whole specification: nothing else is graded and nothing is hidden from you.

`buildRequest(config)` turns a config object into a request object with exactly four keys.

- `method` - `config.method` uppercased, or `"GET"` when it is absent.
- `url` - `config.baseUrl` and `config.path` joined by exactly one `/`, however many slashes each side brings.
- `headers` - always `Accept: "application/json"`; plus `Authorization: "Bearer <token>"` when `config.token` is a non-empty string; plus `Content-Type: "application/json"` when there is a body. A header that does not apply is an absent key, never an empty one.
- `body` - `JSON.stringify(config.body)` when `config.body` is given, otherwise `null`.

`parseResponse(raw)` takes `{ status, body }`, where `body` is text, and returns one of two shapes.

- `{ ok: true, status, data }` for a status from 200 to 299, where `data` is the parsed body, or `null` when the body is empty.
- `{ ok: false, status, error }` for anything else, where `error` is the parsed body's `message` when it has one and `"HTTP " + status` when it does not.
- A body that is not valid JSON gives `{ ok: false, status, error: "Malformed response body" }` whatever the status was.

`shouldRetry(response, attempt)` takes a **parsed** response and the 1-based number of the attempt just made, and returns a boolean. Retry a status of 429 or 500 and above; never retry anything else, never retry a successful response, and never retry once `attempt` has reached 3.

`backoffDelay(attempt)` returns the milliseconds to wait after attempt number `attempt`: 100, doubling each time - 100, 200, 400, 800 - capped at 800, and 0 for an attempt below 1.

`runRequest(transport, config)` is what the tests call. It builds the request once, calls `transport(request)`, parses what comes back, and then either returns or retries. **`await` the transport**: a test may hand you one that answers immediately and one that answers with a promise. It never sleeps - it records what `backoffDelay` said and hands that list back. The result is the parsed response plus two keys.

- `attempts` - how many times the transport was called.
- `delays` - the waits between those calls, so three attempts carry two delays.

A success is therefore `{ ok: true, status, data, attempts, delays }` and a failure is `{ ok: false, status, error, attempts, delays }`. Nothing else is added and nothing is left out.

tests.input: (req) => ({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify(req) }), { baseUrl: "https://api.test/", path: "users/7", method: "post", token: "k-42", body: { name: "Mira" } }

(function () { let i = 0; const seq = [{ status: 500, body: "" }, { status: 500, body: "" }, { status: 200, body: '{"id":7}' }]; return () => seq[i++]; })(), { baseUrl: "https://api.test", path: "/users/7" }
() => ({ status: 404, body: '{"message":"No such user"}' }), { baseUrl: "https://api.test", path: "/users/99" }

(function () { let i = 0; const seq = [{ status: 429, body: '{"message":"Slow down"}' }, { status: 200, body: '{"id":7}' }]; return () => seq[i++]; })(), { baseUrl: "https://api.test", path: "/users/7" }
async (req) => ({ status: 201, body: JSON.stringify({ created: true, sent: req.body }) }), { baseUrl: "https://api.test", path: "/users", method: "POST", body: { name: "Kel" } }

() => ({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ delays: [backoffDelay(0), backoffDelay(1), backoffDelay(2), backoffDelay(3), backoffDelay(9)], retry: [shouldRetry({ ok: false, status: 500 }, 1), shouldRetry({ ok: false, status: 500 }, 3), shouldRetry({ ok: false, status: 429 }, 2), shouldRetry({ ok: false, status: 404 }, 1), shouldRetry({ ok: true, status: 200 }, 1)] }) }), { baseUrl: "https://api.test", path: "/probe" }

trial.explain:
The shape is the lesson: every rule lives in exactly one function, and the only impure thing in the design - the network - arrives as an argument. That is what makes a retry policy testable at all. No real server will hand you two 503s and then a 200 on demand, in a millisecond, identically every time, so a client that calls `fetch` inline can only ever have its happy path tested and its interesting half hoped about.

Three details decide whether this survives a real API. Parsing inside a `try` matters because a failing gateway answers with HTML rather than JSON, and a bare `JSON.parse` turns a 502 into a `SyntaxError` thrown from somewhere that has nothing to do with the cause. Retrying only 429 and 5xx matters because a 404 fails identically forever, so retrying it merely triples the user's wait before showing the same message. And returning the delays instead of sleeping them keeps the runner honest - the wait schedule becomes a value a test can assert on rather than time nobody can observe.

The cap is the quiet one. Without it a client meeting a permanently broken server retries until something else gives up, and a fleet of such clients turns one server's bad minute into an outage - which is also why the wait doubles instead of staying flat.
